props.title: Last Tango in Paris
props.initialSlug: Volatile affair ignites passion and tragedy in Paris

sections.content: Last Tango in Paris stands as one of cinema's most controversial masterpieces. Bernardo Bertolucci's raw exploration of sexual obsession and grief features Marlon Brando in perhaps his most vulnerable performance as Paul, an American widower who enters into an anonymous sexual relationship with young Parisian Jeanne (Maria Schneider). The film's infamous butter scene sparked global outrage and censorship, but more disturbing was the later revelation that Schneider wasn't fully informed about the scene beforehand, raising serious ethical questions about directorial abuse that echo through films like Blue Is the Warmest Color (2013).

sections.content: The film's visual style, crafted by cinematographer Vittorio Storaro, influenced a generation of filmmakers. The muted colors and shadowy Parisian apartments create a claustrophobic atmosphere that would later inspire works like 9½ Weeks (1986) and Eyes Wide Shut (1999). Bertolucci's use of handheld cameras and natural lighting helped establish a new visual language for depicting intimate human drama, seen later in films like Blue Valentine (2010).

Brando's improvisational approach, particularly in the scene where he mourns his dead wife, set new standards for method acting in cinema. His raw emotional display influenced performances in later films like Shame (2011) and A Single Man (2009), where grief and sexuality intertwine in similarly complex ways. sections.content: The film's exploration of power dynamics and emotional manipulation resonates in contemporary works like Nymphomaniac (2013) and The Piano Teacher (2001). Modern filmmakers continue grappling with the ethical implications of depicting explicit sexuality, as seen in debates surrounding Blue Is the Warmest Color (2013) and Love (2015).
